Aesthetics
During the mining operations, the spoil banks, draglines, loading equipment, coal stockpiles and conveyor belts will intrude upon the natural scenic character of the area. These intrusions may be aesthetically offensive to many people as they view the area.
The restored areas will be characterized by a recontoured and reclaimed landscape which masks the former overburden piles. If fully adequate reclamation is accomplished, the appearance may not be displeasing in itself, but the texture, lines and land forms will look unnatural among the more primitive surrounding land. Distinctive and unique land forms such as balanced caprock will be gone, substantially reducing the visual experience. The resulting view, though it may be uniform and pastoral, may be less pleasing to some people than the original view.
Historical and Archaeological Sites
Even if coal developers meet all their legal responsibilities, there is no complete assurance that undiscovered sites will not be overlooked and destroyed. This lack of assurance implies that some loss of archaeological value is unavoidable if undiscovered sites do, in fact, exist.
Noise
A large increase in noise level will be unavoidable and can be expected to be more widespread at the high level rate of production as compared to the low rate. As discussed in Chapter III, the major effects will be felt by the workers (approximately 390 and 540 production employees at the low and high level respectively) and by those living or having business within about a mile of the mine.
